newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK rate rise heals Clarke and George rift.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK rate rise heals Clarke and George rift.

text.p: The rift between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England was partly healed on Wednesday when Clarke delivered a surprise quarter-point rate rise, just months before a general election.

But while the rate rise enhanced the finance minister's reputation as a prudent manager of the economy, City economists said the Bank of England and the country's move towards greater central bank independence were the main victors.
Together, they have managed to push inflation up the political agenda, forcing Clarke to raise the cost of borrowing to keep a check on price pressures.

"The Bank has come out of this very well. For the first time it looks like it is making a real contribution to domestic policy in run up to an election instead of being forced to shout from the sidelines," said Stewart.

The rate rise has gone some way to heal the rift between Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George. The two men fell out over the quarter-point rate cut in June, George arguing the economy was in no need of extra stimulation.

The subsequent run of data proved the central bank governor right and on Wednesday Clarke was forced to reverse the cut, just four months later and well before its effects were fully felt in the economy.
The Bank publicly lost the argument in May 1995 when its unheeded call for a half point rate rise was followed a by a run of weak economic data. Now it can now claim an equaliser.

Officials at Threadneedle Street have planned and executed their tactics very carefully, using the August inflation report to raise doubts that the government would hit its tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
Officials also managed to up the ante by stating in the summer that they were already discussing the merits of a pre-emptive rate rise.
Economists said the rate rise has bolstered Britain's fledgling monetary framework.
Set up in early 1993 to help protect interest rates from political meddling, fears have grown in the City that it would fall apart as the election approached.

The ruling Conservatives still trail opposition Labour by over 20 points in the polls and Clarke is under intense political pressure to deliver a strong sense of national economic well-being before the election, which must be held by May 1997.
Many economists thought Clarke would bow to political pressure and refuse to raise the cost of borrowing before the election whatever the inflationary pressures.
"But the new policy framework is clearly acting as a constraint and Clarke is listening to the Governor's advise," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.

Relations between Clarke and George may be more harmonious, at least for a while. In the summer, sources close to the Bank said officials were growing frustrated with Clarke's dismissive attitude towards their advise.
The Bank has a purely advisory role in setting interest rates, but Clarke has criticised it in recent month's, saying it is too gloomy in its inflation projections.
But with underlying inflation creeping up again -- it edged up to 2.9 percent in September after spending four months stuck at 2.8 percent -- Clarke may have to eat his words.
City economists said the Chancellor has a long way to go before he goes down in history as the minister who put economics before politics and fortified Britain's tenuous inflation credentials.
"But the real test will come next year," said Mackie.

George is unlikely to be satisfied with a paltry quarter-point rise. As the consumer-led recovery picks up pace later this year and next he is sure to seek another tightening, possibly as soon as January.
"The Governor is definately going to come back and ask for more in January and it will be then we see how Clarke responds to the pressure," said Mackie.
